label: Axis (Lecture 14)
rows: Normal
-30 to +90 degrees: lead I UP, aVF UP.
Left axis deviation
Beyond -30: lead I UP, aVF DOWN. Causes include left anterior fascicular block, past inferior infarction, ventricular pacing.
Right axis deviation
Beyond +90: lead I DOWN, aVF UP. Causes include chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, pulmonary embolism, dextrocardia, left posterior fascicular block; NORMAL IN CHILDREN.
Extreme (no man's land)
-90 to 180: lead I DOWN, aVF DOWN. Causes include ventricular arrhythmia, hyperkalemia, lead transposition. ★ Wide tachycardia + extreme axis → think VENTRICULAR TACHYCARDIA.
Quick method
Lead I and aVF; is each QRS mostly positive or mostly negative?
Slide errors
Slide 22's right-axis quadrant is drawn reversed (I down, aVF up is correct). Slide 21 lists left ventricular hypertrophy under right axis; it causes LEFT axis deviation.

label: Bundle Branch Blocks
rows: Both
QRS 0.12 s or LONGER (3 small boxes). V1 decides the side.
★ J point rule (V1)
Travel BACK from the J point: first deflection NEGATIVE = LEFT; POSITIVE = RIGHT. (Left blinker goes down.)
Left bundle branch block
rS in V1; NOTCHED lateral QRS (I, aVL, V5, V6; double QRS best in V6); NO lateral Q waves.
Right bundle branch block
rSR in V1; SLURRED S waves in I, aVL, V5, V6. Bunny ears unreliable: many V1 shapes, but always ends positive.
Why wide
Blocked side waits for slow MYOCYTE-TO-MYOCYTE spread; ventricles depolarize in SEQUENCE (two-QRS phenomenon).
Left block physiology
Right ventricle first; septal fascicle blocked → septal Q waves lost laterally.
Incomplete block
Not in the deck or recording; not quizzed.

label: Fascicular Blocks
rows: Left bundle
Splits into ANTERIOR, POSTERIOR and SEPTAL fascicles.
Left anterior (hemiblock)
LEFT axis, q in I and r in III (q1r3), II and III negative. ★ MOST COMMON intraventricular conduction abnormality in ACUTE MYOCARDIAL INFARCTION.
Left posterior (hemiblock)
RIGHT axis, r in I and q in III (r1q3), III positive; lead II not significant. FAR LESS common.

label: Atrial Enlargement
rows: Enlargement means
STRETCHING that DILATES a chamber; most seen in the ATRIA (valve disease, pulmonary hypertension, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, pulmonary embolism).
Right (P PULMONALE)
Limb leads: upright P TALLER than 2.5 mm. V1: biphasic, LARGER POSITIVE first part.
Left (P MITRALE)
Limb leads: HUMPED P ≥0.12 s, humps ≥0.04 s apart. V1: biphasic, LARGE NEGATIVE terminal part.
One lead is enough
Either criterion in ONE lead confirms it.

label: Ventricular Hypertrophy
rows: Hypertrophy means
THICKENING of the muscle that makes the chamber SMALLER.
Right ventricular hypertrophy
MORE R than S in V1 and V2. Supported by right atrial enlargement, right axis deviation, STRAIN. Excluded by RIGHT BUNDLE BRANCH BLOCK, posterior infarction, age under 7 or 8.
Strain pattern
ST from the J point into an INVERTED, ASYMMETRICAL T wave, V1 and V2.
Left ventricular hypertrophy
LEFT axis; DEEP S in V1 and V2, TALL R in I, aVL, V5, V6. Any ONE: S (V1/V2) + R (V5/V6) ≥35 mm; R in aVL >12 mm; any chest lead >45 mm.
★ Infarction mimic

Left ventricular hypertrophy is the MOST COMMON: CONCAVE upward ST elevation V1–V3 + lateral T inversion. Others: pericarditis, early repolarization, Brugada, left bundle branch block and ventricular pacing, hypothermia.

label: The Systematic 12-Lead
rows: Order
General impression → calibration → AXIS → QRS (wide? blocks?) → hypertrophy/enlargement → ST and T changes.
Standard calibration
ONE big box wide, TWO big boxes tall.
Name the rhythm first
A bundle branch block is NOT a rhythm: "sinus tachycardia with a left bundle branch block."
